answer:
1. The animation shows how inflation wears down the buying power of a fixed annuity payment. It compares a level (flat) check with a rising check that has a cost-of-living increase. The label is "US consumer prices (CPI-U)". It is marked "illustrative" and "US only · history, not a forecast".

2. In frame 1, both checks start at the same size, "10 crates" of goods. Over time, prices rise. By frames 3–6, the level check buys only about 6 crates in 10, or 60.9% of what it first bought. The rising check, which grows about 2% a year, still buys about 9 in 10, or 90.4%. The crate bars shrink and grey out to show this. Frames 5 and 6 add that each check is measured against its own first check, in purchasing power and not dollars. Frame 6 also notes that starting sizes are not modeled.

3. A flat payment loses real purchasing power as prices climb. A payment that rises each year keeps much more of its purchasing power, though not all of it, on this historical example. The animation doesn't say that a rising payment is worth more overall. It says nothing about the two options' starting payments.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer in my position, 64 and about to retire, might take away that inflation matters over a long retirement. I'd want to ask what the rising-check option's lower starting payment costs me, and I'd compare the two options on that basis.

5. The animation did not suggest the advice. It is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the comparison and warns that it is historical, US-only, illustrative and not a forecast. It doesn't tell viewers to choose either option.
